triage.name: Neonatal sepsis
triage.reason: Young infant with nonspecific instability, poor feeding and temperature instability; a core diagnosis reached by history, exam, cultures and CSF studies, with many mimics.

demographics: More common in preterm and low birth weight infants
Early-onset disease occurs within the first 7 days of life, most often within 24 hours of birth
Late-onset disease occurs after 7 days and before 90 days of age

risk_factors.text: Preterm birth or low birth weight
Maternal urinary tract infection or bacteremia
Invasive procedures, central lines, or prolonged hospitalization

exposures: Invasive procedures or central venous catheters

chief_complaints.text: My baby is very sleepy and hard to wake

hpi.onset: Gradual or sudden; early-onset sepsis appears within the first 7 days of life, often within 24 hours of birth, while late-onset sepsis appears after 7 days and before 90 days of age
hpi.progression: Symptoms may worsen rapidly; initially subtle signs such as poor feeding and sleepiness can progress to respiratory distress, temperature instability, and shock
hpi.quality: Nonspecific; includes poor feeding, lethargy, temperature instability, respiratory distress, and jaundice
hpi.severity: Variable; can be mild initially but may progress to severe sepsis or septic shock
hpi.timing: Continuous or intermittent; often worse around feeding times

atypical.how_it_differs: Preterm infants may present with apnea, bradycardia, and temperature instability rather than fever or focal signs.
Infants with immunodeficiency may have a blunted inflammatory response and present with subtle or absent fever.

general.mild: Well-appearing or mildly unwell infant; alert but feeding poorly; may be warm or slightly cool to touch
general.moderate: Unwell, fussy or drowsy, poor tone, feeding poorly, temperature unstable
general.severe: Ill-appearing, lethargic or inconsolable, poor perfusion, respiratory distress, temperature instability
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, limp, apneic or gasping, mottled or pale, signs of shock

labs.caveat: May be low, normal or high; neutropenia and leukopenia are common in neonatal sepsis and do not exclude it.
A left shift with immature-to-total neutrophil ratio above 0.2 supports the diagnosis.
Thrombocytopenia is a common and early sign of neonatal sepsis and also raises concern for disseminated intravascular coagulation.
May be normal at presentation and rises over 6–24 hours; serial values are more useful than a single level.
Rises earlier than CRP but has a physiologic spike in the first 48 hours of life, so age-specific norms are needed.
Hypoglycemia is common and must be corrected immediately; it also worsens neurologic injury.
Elevated lactate with poor perfusion supports septic shock and guides resuscitation.
Metabolic acidosis from poor perfusion or anaerobic metabolism.
Normal neonatal CSF white count can be up to about 20–30/µL; a predominance of neutrophils is abnormal.
Normal neonatal CSF protein is higher than in older children (up to about 90–150 mg/dL depending on age).
Compare with the simultaneous serum glucose; a CSF-to-serum ratio below about 0.6 is abnormal.
Low fibrinogen with prolonged clotting times supports disseminated intravascular coagulation.
Jaundice may be the presenting sign; check whether it is direct or indirect and whether it is hemolytic.
Neonatal creatinine reflects maternal values early on; a rising or persistently high value suggests renal injury.
A urinary tract infection can be the source of late-onset sepsis.

imaging.preferred_when: Respiratory distress, apnea, or suspected pneumonia

imaging.preferred_when: Abdominal distension, feeding intolerance, or suspected necrotizing enterocolitis
Preterm infants, suspected meningitis, seizures, or suspected intraventricular hemorrhage

findings.text: Ventriculomegaly or echogenic periventricular white matter

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected congenital heart disease, persistent shock, or a murmur

findings.text: Reduced ventricular function or pericardial effusion

initial.why: White count, differential and platelets; a left shift or thrombocytopenia supports sepsis
Glucose, electrolytes and renal function; hypoglycemia is common and must be corrected
Assesses perfusion and severity of shock
Baseline inflammatory marker; serial values help monitor response
Definitive test; obtain before starting antibiotics from two sites if possible
Lumbar puncture for cell count, protein, glucose and culture; meningitis is common and changes management
initial.only_if: the infant is stable enough to tolerate the procedure

initial.why: Looks for pneumonia or a respiratory source
initial.only_if: respiratory distress, apnea, or abnormal lung exam

supporting.why: Rises earlier than CRP; may help decide duration of antibiotics
Screens for coagulopathy or disseminated intravascular coagulation
Screens for coagulopathy or disseminated intravascular coagulation
Screens for coagulopathy or disseminated intravascular coagulation
Low values support disseminated intravascular coagulation
supporting.only_if: bleeding or suspected disseminated intravascular coagulation

supporting.why: Evaluates jaundice, which may be the presenting sign
Looks for intraventricular hemorrhage or ventriculomegaly
supporting.only_if: preterm infant, seizures, or suspected meningitis

supporting.why: Rules out congenital heart disease as a mimic of septic shock

not_indicated.only_if: no abdominal distension or feeding intolerance

not_indicated.why: Not routine in a term infant without neurologic findings
Not routine unless congenital heart disease is suspected
No role in the diagnosis of neonatal sepsis
Not part of the acute sepsis workup

decision_points: Obtain blood culture before starting antibiotics; do not delay antibiotics for the lumbar puncture in an unstable infant
Lumbar puncture is deferred in an unstable infant and performed once stabilized
Correct hypoglycemia and treat shock with fluids and vasoactive support while cultures are pending
A normal CBC, CRP and blood culture do not exclude early-onset sepsis; antibiotics are often continued based on clinical risk factors

differential.name: Respiratory distress syndrome of prematurity
differential.why_considered: Preterm infant with grunting, retractions, tachypnea and hypoxia in the first hours of life

history: Preterm birth, often before 34 weeks
Symptoms begin immediately after birth and worsen over the first 24-48 hours
No maternal fever or chorioamnionitis
exam: Diffuse grunting and retractions with poor air entry bilaterally
No lethargy or poor perfusion early on
labs: Blood culture negative
CRP and procalcitonin remain low or fall on serial testing
Blood gas shows hypoxemia with respiratory acidosis rather than a septic metabolic picture
imaging: Chest x-ray shows low lung volumes with diffuse ground-glass opacities and air bronchograms
No focal consolidation or pleural effusion

differential.name: Transient tachypnea of the newborn
differential.why_considered: Term or late-preterm infant with tachypnea and mild respiratory distress shortly after delivery

history: Term or late-preterm infant
Often delivered by cesarean section or with rapid delivery
Respiratory symptoms begin within hours of birth and improve over 24-72 hours
exam: Tachypnea with mild retractions but good air entry
No temperature instability or poor perfusion
labs: Blood culture negative
Inflammatory markers normal
Mild respiratory acidosis that resolves
imaging: Chest x-ray shows perihilar streaking, fluid in the fissures, and mild hyperinflation
Findings clear on repeat film within 1-2 days

differential.name: Congenital heart disease with ductal-dependent circulation
differential.why_considered: Neonate with shock, poor perfusion, acidosis and respiratory distress that can mimic septic shock
differential.trigger: Shock or cyanosis that does not improve with fluids and antibiotics, or a murmur with differential cyanosis

history: Symptoms may appear as the ductus arteriosus closes, often on day 2-14 of life
Antenatal ultrasound may have shown a cardiac anomaly
No maternal infectious risk factors
exam: Murmur, single second heart sound, or differential cyanosis (upper extremity pink, lower extremity blue)
Weak or absent femoral pulses in coarctation
labs: Blood culture negative
Hyperoxia test shows no rise in PaO2 with 100% oxygen
Metabolic acidosis may be present but inflammatory markers are normal
imaging: Echocardiogram identifies the structural defect and ductal dependency
Chest x-ray may show cardiomegaly or abnormal pulmonary vascularity

differential.name: Metabolic disorder (inborn error of metabolism)
differential.why_considered: Neonate with lethargy, poor feeding, vomiting, acidosis and shock after an initial well period
differential.trigger: Deterioration after a symptom-free interval with severe metabolic acidosis, hypoglycemia, or hyperammonemia

history: Well for the first hours to days of life, then progressive lethargy and poor feeding
Consanguinity or a family history of neonatal death or metabolic disease
Symptoms worsen with feeding
exam: No fever; temperature may be normal or low
labs: Severe metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap
Hyperammonemia, hypoglycemia, or abnormal acylcarnitine profile
Blood culture negative; inflammatory markers normal
imaging: Cranial ultrasound or MRI may show cerebral edema or white matter changes

differential.name: Viral infection (enterovirus, parechovirus, HSV)
differential.why_considered: Young infant with fever, poor feeding, irritability and sometimes a rash or seizures
differential.trigger: Fever with vesicular rash, seizures, or CSF pleocytosis with negative bacterial cultures

history: Seasonal pattern (enterovirus in summer/fall)
Maternal history of HSV or genital lesions
Sick contacts with viral illness
exam: Vesicular rash (HSV), or nonspecific maculopapular rash (enterovirus)
Irritability or seizures out of proportion to fever
labs: CSF PCR positive for enterovirus, parechovirus, or HSV
Bacterial cultures negative
CSF may show lymphocytic pleocytosis; HSV may show red blood cells and elevated protein
imaging: MRI brain may show temporal lobe changes in HSV encephalitis

differential.name: Necrotizing enterocolitis
differential.why_considered: Preterm infant with abdominal distension, feeding intolerance, temperature instability and apnea

history: Preterm, often with enteral feeds started
Feeding intolerance and bilious emesis
Bloody stools
exam: Abdominal distension, tenderness, or erythema of the abdominal wall
labs: Thrombocytopenia, metabolic acidosis, and elevated inflammatory markers
Blood culture may be positive but is not diagnostic
imaging: Abdominal x-ray shows pneumatosis intestinalis, portal venous gas, or free air
Dilated bowel loops with thickened walls

differential.name: Urinary tract infection
differential.why_considered: Young infant with fever, poor feeding and no localizing signs; a common source of late-onset sepsis

history: Age typically after 7 days and before 90 days
No respiratory or neurologic symptoms
May have a history of antenatal hydronephrosis
labs: Urinalysis positive for leukocyte esterase and nitrites
Urine culture grows a single organism
Blood culture may be negative or positive
imaging: Renal ultrasound may show hydronephrosis or structural abnormality
VCUG if recurrent or abnormal ultrasound

severity.mild: Well-appearing or mildly unwell infant with poor feeding, temperature instability, and no respiratory distress or shock; normal perfusion and alert
severity.moderate: Unwell infant with fever or hypothermia, lethargy, tachypnea, tachycardia, and mild perfusion abnormalities but still maintaining blood pressure
severity.severe: Ill-appearing infant with respiratory distress, apnea, poor perfusion, hypotension, metabolic acidosis, and need for respiratory or vasoactive support
severity.critical: Septic shock with refractory hypotension, multi-organ failure, disseminated intravascular coagulation, or meningitis with neurologic compromise

red_flags.meaning: Respiratory failure or central apnea from sepsis; requires immediate airway support
Septic shock; needs fluid resuscitation and vasoactive support

red_flags.finding: Bulging fontanelle, seizures, or nuchal rigidity
red_flags.meaning: Meningitis or raised intracranial pressure; lumbar puncture and antibiotics urgently

red_flags.finding: Petechiae or bleeding from puncture sites
red_flags.meaning: Disseminated intravascular coagulation; check platelets and clotting studies
Poor reserve or sepsis; correct immediately to prevent neurologic injury
Poor perfusion and anaerobic metabolism; indicates severe sepsis or shock

complications.name: Neurodevelopmental impairment
clues: History of meningitis or septic shock

special_populations.differences: Preterm infants may present with apnea, bradycardia, and temperature instability rather than fever or focal signs; they are at higher risk for intraventricular hemorrhage and necrotizing enterocolitis.
Infants with immunodeficiency may have a blunted inflammatory response and present with subtle or absent fever and normal white count.

key_questions.question: How old is the baby now, and how many days old was he or she when the symptoms started?
key_questions.looking_for: Age under 90 days; onset within the first 7 days suggests early-onset sepsis, onset after 7 days suggests late-onset sepsis

key_questions.question: How is the baby feeding compared with usual — is he or she taking less, refusing feeds, or too sleepy to feed?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor feeding or feeding intolerance, a common and early nonspecific sign

key_questions.question: Has the baby's temperature been high, low, or swinging between the two?
key_questions.looking_for: Temperature instability — fever or hypothermia; neonates may not mount a fever

key_questions.question: How alert and responsive is the baby — is he or she sleepier than usual, floppy, or hard to wake?
key_questions.looking_for: Lethargy or reduced responsiveness, suggesting systemic illness

key_questions.question: Has the baby had any pauses in breathing, grunting, flaring, or fast breathing?
key_questions.looking_for: Apnea, grunting, nasal flaring, retractions, or tachypnea — respiratory signs of sepsis

key_questions.question: Has the baby had any vomiting, abdominal swelling, or blood in the stool?
key_questions.looking_for: Vomiting, abdominal distension, or bloody stools, which raise concern for necrotizing enterocolitis

key_questions.question: Has the baby had any abnormal movements, twitching, or staring spells?
key_questions.looking_for: Seizures, which suggest meningitis or metabolic derangement

key_questions.question: Has the baby's skin looked yellow, pale, mottled, or spotted?
How was the pregnancy and delivery — was the baby born early, and how long after the water broke was he or she born?
key_questions.looking_for: Preterm birth, prolonged rupture of membranes (18 hours or more), or cesarean delivery

key_questions.question: Did the mother have a fever, chorioamnionitis, a urinary tract infection, or a positive group B Streptococcus swab during pregnancy?
key_questions.looking_for: Maternal infectious risk factors for early-onset sepsis

key_questions.question: Did the mother receive antibiotics in labor, and was group B Streptococcus screening done?
key_questions.looking_for: Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis, which lowers but does not eliminate risk

key_questions.question: Has the baby had any lines, tubes, procedures, or a long hospital stay since birth?
key_questions.looking_for: Invasive devices or prolonged hospitalization, risk factors for late-onset sepsis

key_questions.question: Does the baby have any known congenital anomalies, immune problems, or prior infections?
key_questions.looking_for: Comorbidities that increase risk or alter presentation

key_questions.question: Is anyone at home or in close contact sick with a fever, rash, or cold sores?
key_questions.looking_for: Viral exposures such as HSV or enterovirus that can mimic bacterial sepsis

key_questions.question: Has the baby been immunized or had any recent shots?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent immunization, which can cause fever and irritability and is a mimic

reasoning_points: Age under 90 days with nonspecific signs such as poor feeding, lethargy, and temperature instability
Timing distinguishes early-onset (within the first 7 days, often within 24 hours of birth) from late-onset (after 7 days and before 90 days) disease
Maternal and perinatal risk factors: preterm birth, group B Streptococcus colonization, prolonged rupture of membranes, maternal fever or chorioamnionitis
Examination findings of temperature instability, poor feeding, lethargy, respiratory distress or apnea, and poor perfusion
Blood culture obtained before antibiotics is the definitive test; a normal CBC, CRP, or culture does not exclude early-onset sepsis
Lumbar puncture for CSF cell count, protein, glucose, and culture because meningitis is common and changes management
Urine culture is important in late-onset disease as a source
Hypoglycemia and shock must be corrected immediately while cultures are pending

Look-alikes considered and addressed: respiratory distress syndrome, transient tachypnea of the newborn, congenital heart disease, inborn errors of metabolism, viral infection, necrotizing enterocolitis, and urinary tract infection

easy: Preterm infant with maternal group B Streptococcus colonization and prolonged rupture of membranes
Onset within the first 24 hours of life with poor feeding, lethargy, and temperature instability
Ill-appearing infant with tachypnea, grunting, and poor perfusion
Clear maternal risk factors and a positive blood culture
medium: Term infant with only poor feeding and mild temperature instability and no focal signs
Late-onset disease at 3 to 6 weeks of age with fever and no localizing source
Normal white count and normal CRP at presentation despite clinical sepsis
Jaundice as the presenting sign without respiratory distress
hard: Preterm infant presenting with apnea and bradycardia rather than fever
Infant with an inborn error of metabolism who was well initially and then deteriorated after feeding
Infant with ductal-dependent congenital heart disease presenting with shock that mimics septic shock
Infant with HSV or enterovirus infection with seizures and a vesicular rash
Infant with necrotizing enterocolitis and abdominal distension masking sepsis
